title: Target Practice on the Molecular Scale
body_text: I’ve remarked before that one of the big differences in the modern chemical literature versus the “back when I was in grad school” era (which for me is the 1980s, dang it all) is that we now can do a lot more at smaller scales. Detailed pictures of surface and single-molecule phenomena just didn’t exist, for the most part, and we just continue to get better at those things. This new paper is a good illustration. The authors are looking at a reaction on a copper surface, Cu(110) to be precise). That surface has ridges in it like a plowed field, as opposed to the relatively flat plane of the Cu(111) surface, and this has already been used to try to direct the geometry of bimolecular reactions. In such cases, trifluoromethyl iodide is deposited onto this copper surface at very low temperatures, and each molecule then decomposes into an iodine atom and a chemically absorbed CF3 fragment. Those can be dissociated in turn by electron impact into a single F atom and a CF2 “projectile” that (by scanning tunneling microscopy) ends up flying up to 12 Angstroms away from the original trifluoromethyl source. Interestingly, these always seem to fly along the copper furrows on the surface; you get some real directional control. In this work, the authors introduce (the rather large and roughly linear) dibromoterfluorene molecule (DBTF) as a target for these difluoro cannonballs. They note that the bromine atoms at the ends make the molecules easy to spot and to manipulate by STM, and that its shape let you see just how it’s sitting on the copper surface (there are several orientations available as well, which also helps). The paper shows the four main ones as determined by STM imaging - one lying straight across the copper ridges, another lying parallel to them, and two others that assemble at different angles in between (one at about 40 degrees off horizontal and the other about 60 degrees off). They hit such molecules with an electron pulse to dissociate one of the bromines off an end, leaving a “BTFyl” radical chemically absorbed onto the copper. This process seems to preserve the initial orientation, albeit knocking the molecule a couple of Angstroms back as it happens. DFT calculations suggest that the radical is bonded to a single copper atom in these cases that gets pulled up about 1.3 Å by that interaction. (See, I told you we’ve gotten better at understanding what goes on at surfaces!) So that sets things up to fire CF2 groups at these species in all sorts of orientation, using the abovementioned copper furrows as aiming devices. And when this happens, each time the authors go in with the STM tip to confirm whether or not a new bond has formed. The CF2 and BTFyl species end up next to each other most every time, but sometimes you can reach down and physically push the CF2 away, indicating that no bond formed; they’re just sitting there side by side. But other times when you push, the whole ensemble moves as a new unit. You can drop the STM tip into the center of the terfluorene molecule and shove it around from there, and the CF2 next to it drags right along in any direction along with it, because it has indeed formed a new bond. When the results of dozens of such experiments are collected, it becomes clear that most of the interactions are unproductive and do not form bonds. And that’s because they’re not hitting the BTFyl target at its exact reactive spot on one end. The only bond-forming collisions take place right there, and you can even divide those up into which copper row directed them there (two of them will work to deliver things within bond-forming range, but no others, and those two seem to be effective partly because of the somewhat-altered copper atom spacing mentioned above. So there really are very tight trajectories and geometries that constrain bond-forming reactions, as other lines of evidence have indicated over the years. But this is an extremely vivid and direct illustration of this effect, and shows the sorts of factors we’ll have to consider if we want to control on-surface reactions more meaningfully. Given the number of important catalytic processes that happen at such surfaces, we’re going to need all the knowledge like this that we can get.
